title: Identity, Mutability & Copying
html:
Every Python value is an object with an identity, a type and a value. Knowing which objects are shared, which can change, and how copies work explains most “spooky action at a distance” bugs.

Object — a chunk of memory with an identity (id(x) — fixed for its lifetime), a type (type(x) — decides what it can do) and a value (which may or may not be allowed to change).

Identity, type, value

QuestionOperator / functionCalls
Same value?a == ba.__eq__(b) — can be customised
Same object?a is bcompares identities — can't be overridden
Which object?id(a)an integer unique among live objects (the address in CPython)
What kind?type(a), isinstance(a, T)isinstance also accepts subclasses
Key point

Use is only for singletons: x is None, x is True, sentinel objects. For everything else, compare values with ==.

Small-int cache & string interning

CPython pre-creates the integers −5…256 and reuses (interns) many identifier-like strings, so equal values may happen to be the same object. That is an implementation detail — never write code whose result depends on it.

Classic bug

if name is "admin": may work in a REPL test and fail in production. Python 3.8+ even emits a SyntaxWarning for is with a literal.

Mutable vs immutable

Immutable — value can never changeMutable — can change in place
int, float, complex, bool, str, byteslist, dict, set, bytearray
tuple, frozenset, range, Nonemost user-defined class instances

“Changing” an immutable object really creates a new object and rebinds the name. Mutating a mutable object is visible through every name that refers to it.

Key point

Hashability follows immutability: dict keys and set items must be hashable, and a hash is only safe if the value can't change. That's why tuple and frozenset can be keys but list and set can't.

Aliasing through function calls

Do

Return a new object from functions by default; if you must mutate an argument, say so in the name/docstring (sort_in_place) and return None like list.sort.

Avoid

Silently mutating arguments the caller still uses — or storing a caller's list inside an object without copying it.

Shallow vs deep copy

WayResult
b = aNo copy — just another name
a[:], list(a), a.copy(), dict(d), d.copy(), set(s)Shallow: new outer container, same inner objects
copy.copy(x)Shallow copy of any object
copy.deepcopy(x)Deep: recursively copies everything reachable
Key point

Immutable leaves (int, str, tuple of immutables) are never really copied — sharing them is safe, so deepcopy reuses them.

deepcopy handles cycles; __copy__ / __deepcopy__

deepcopy keeps a memo dict of objects already copied, so shared references stay shared and cycles don't recurse forever. Classes can customise copying with __copy__ and __deepcopy__(self, memo).

Puzzle: a tuple that changes

t[0] += [3] is t[0] = t[0].__iadd__([3]): the list is extended in place first, then storing it back into the tuple raises. The error is real — and so is the mutation.

What is the difference between is and ==?

== asks whether two objects have equal values (it calls __eq__). is asks whether two names refer to the same object (identical id). Use is for None and other singletons, == for everything else.

Why does a is b return True for 256 but False for 1000?

CPython caches small integers from −5 to 256, so every 256 is the same object. Larger ints created at run time are separate objects. It's an implementation detail — compare numbers with ==.

When do you need a deep copy?

When the object contains mutable inner objects (lists of lists, dicts of lists, objects holding lists) and you want the copy to be fully independent. A shallow copy is enough for a flat list of immutable values.
